title: Population & Urban Issues
description: Where people live and why — population distribution and density, population pyramids, birth and death rates, migration, urbanisation and the challenges of rapidly growing cities.

notes.heading: Population Distribution and Density
notes.body: Population distribution is the pattern of where people live across the Earth's surface — and it is extremely uneven. Some areas are densely populated (crowded), others are sparsely populated (almost empty). Population density is the measure used to compare places: number of people divided by the area, usually people per square kilometre. Worked example: a country with 12 million people in 40 000 km² has a density of 12 000 000 ÷ 40 000 = 300 people per km². Why is population so uneven? Physical factors: flat, fertile land with a mild climate and reliable water (like river valleys and coastal lowlands) attracts dense settlement; steep mountains, deserts, frozen tundra and dense rainforest repel it. Human factors: jobs, good transport links, trade routes and stable government draw people in; isolation, few jobs and conflict push them away. Densely populated regions include South and East Asia and much of Europe. Sparsely populated regions include the Sahara, the Arctic and the Amazon rainforest. Remember: a large country can have a low density if few people live there — density depends on people AND area.

notes.heading: Population Structure and Population Pyramids
notes.body: Population structure is the make-up of a population by age and gender. It is displayed on a population pyramid — a special bar graph with two back-to-back bars for each age group (cohort): males on the left, females on the right, youngest at the bottom, oldest at the top. The shape tells you a great deal about a country. A wide base means a high birth rate (many children). A pyramid that narrows sharply upwards means high death rates and low life expectancy (few old people). A tall, straight-sided, 'beehive' shape means low birth rates and an ageing population — typical of wealthy countries. A broad top means many elderly people needing care and pensions. Typical shapes: many poorer countries have a true pyramid — wide base, narrow top, high birth rate, high death rate. Wealthier countries have a column or beehive shape — low birth rate, low death rate, many people living into old age. Key groups geographers look at: young dependents (0–15), the working population (16–64), and elderly dependents (65+). The dependency ratio compares dependents to workers. Governments use pyramids to plan: a wide base means more schools will be needed; a wide top means more hospitals, care homes and pensions.

notes.heading: Birth Rates, Death Rates and Natural Increase
notes.body: Population change is measured with rates. The birth rate is the number of live births per 1 000 people per year. The death rate is the number of deaths per 1 000 people per year. Natural increase is the difference: birth rate minus death rate. If births exceed deaths, the population grows naturally; if deaths exceed births, it shrinks (natural decrease). Worked example: a country with a birth rate of 22 and a death rate of 9 has a natural increase of 13 per 1 000, or 1.3% per year. Total population change also includes migration: overall change = natural increase + net migration (immigrants minus emigrants). Rates change as countries develop — a pattern called the demographic transition: poor, rural societies have high birth and death rates; improving medicine and sanitation make death rates fall first, so population grows rapidly; later, education, family planning and city living bring birth rates down, and growth slows. High birth rates are linked to: children needed for farm work, high infant mortality (families have more babies to ensure some survive), lack of education and contraception, and cultural traditions. Death rates fall with clean water, vaccines, better food and healthcare.

notes.heading: Migration: Push and Pull Factors
notes.body: Migration is the movement of people from one place to another to live, either permanently or for a long period. Emigration is leaving a country; immigration is entering one. Net migration is the balance between the two. Geographers explain migration using push and pull factors. Push factors are negatives that drive people away from a place: unemployment, low wages, war and persecution, drought, famine, natural disasters, poor housing and lack of services like schools and hospitals. Pull factors are positives that attract people to a new place: job opportunities, higher wages, better healthcare and education, safety and political stability, family already living there, and a better quality of life. Most migrants move for a combination of both. Common types of migration: rural-to-urban migration (countryside to city, the biggest movement worldwide); international migration (between countries); and forced migration (refugees fleeing war or disaster, with no real choice). Migration has impacts on both ends: the home area may lose young workers but receive money sent back (remittances); the destination gains workers and skills but may face pressure on housing and services.

notes.heading: Urbanisation
notes.body: Urbanisation is the increasing proportion of a country's population living in towns and cities. A settlement is a place where people live, ranging from hamlet → village → town → city → megacity (a city with over 10 million people). In 1800 only about 1 in 20 people worldwide lived in cities; today it is more than half, and the proportion keeps rising — fastest in Africa and Asia. Urbanisation is driven mainly by rural-to-urban migration (people moving for jobs and services — the push of rural poverty and the pull of city opportunity) plus natural increase within cities, because city populations are young. In wealthier countries urbanisation happened during industrialisation in the 1800s, and the pattern is now more complex: suburbanisation (growth of housing at the city edge), counter-urbanisation (people moving back out to villages and commuting in) and re-urbanisation (regenerating inner-city areas). Cities grow because they concentrate opportunity: jobs, universities, hospitals, entertainment and transport. But rapid, unplanned growth — especially in poorer countries — can outstrip a city's ability to provide housing, clean water and services for everyone.

notes.heading: Problems of Rapid City Growth
notes.body: When a city's population grows faster than its housing, jobs and services, serious problems follow. Housing: millions of new arrivals cannot afford formal housing, so they build informal settlements (shanty towns) on empty land — homes made from scrap materials, often with no legal electricity, running water or sanitation, on dangerous sites like steep slopes or floodplains. Employment: there are not enough formal jobs, so many people work in the informal sector — street selling, casual labour, recycling waste — with no contract, fixed wage or security. Traffic congestion: roads built for far fewer vehicles become gridlocked, wasting time and causing air pollution. Pollution and waste: rubbish collection and sewers cannot keep up; waste is dumped in rivers and streets, spreading disease, and smog harms health. Water and sanitation: shared taps and open sewers allow diseases like cholera to spread. Services: schools and clinics are overcrowded, and crime can rise where inequality is extreme. Solutions include: self-help schemes (government provides materials and basic services so residents can improve their own homes), site-and-service projects (plots with water and electricity where people build legally), improving public transport, and building affordable housing. The key idea: growth itself is not the problem — unplanned growth is.

notes.heading: Managing Cities for the Future
notes.body: A sustainable city is one that meets the needs of its people today without damaging the environment or the chances of future generations. As urbanisation continues, planners focus on several strategies. Housing: upgrading informal settlements with water, sewers and legal land titles rather than bulldozing them, because residents have invested their own labour and communities. Transport: investing in reliable, affordable public transport (buses, metro, trams), cycle lanes and pedestrian zones reduces congestion and air pollution; congestion charging discourages car use in city centres. Green space: parks, street trees and green roofs improve air quality, reduce flood risk by absorbing rainwater, and improve mental health. Waste and resources: recycling schemes, clean energy, and treating water and sewage properly protect health. Planning: land-use zoning keeps heavy industry away from homes; building upwards and reusing derelict 'brownfield' land stops cities sprawling onto farmland. Smart growth also means creating jobs and services in smaller towns, so not everyone is pushed towards one giant city. The lesson from cities worldwide is that the most successful solutions involve local communities in decisions — top-down projects without local support usually fail.

flashcards.definition: The pattern of where people live across an area or the world — extremely uneven, with dense and sparse regions.
flashcards.example: People cluster in fertile river valleys, while deserts and high mountains are almost empty.

flashcards.definition: The number of people living in each square kilometre of land, calculated as population ÷ area.
flashcards.example: 600 000 people in 2 000 km² gives a density of 300 people per km².

flashcards.definition: A graph showing population structure: back-to-back bars for males and females in each age group, youngest at the bottom.
flashcards.example: A wide-based pyramid with a narrow top signals a country with a high birth rate and low life expectancy.

flashcards.definition: The number of live births per 1 000 people per year.
flashcards.example: A birth rate of 30 means 30 babies are born each year for every 1 000 people.

flashcards.definition: The difference between birth rate and death rate; positive when births exceed deaths, causing the population to grow.
flashcards.example: Birth rate 25 minus death rate 10 gives natural increase of 15 per 1 000, or 1.5%.

flashcards.definition: The movement of people from one place to another to live, explained by push factors (negatives) and pull factors (positives).
flashcards.example: War pushes people away from a country; jobs and safety pull them towards another.

flashcards.definition: The movement of people from the countryside to towns and cities — the main driver of urbanisation worldwide.
flashcards.example: A young farmer moves to the capital hoping for a factory job and better schools for their children.

flashcards.definition: The increasing proportion of a population living in towns and cities rather than the countryside.
flashcards.example: More than half of the world's people now live in urban areas, up from about 5% in 1800.

flashcards.definition: A city with a population of over 10 million people.
flashcards.example: Megacities are found mainly in Asia, South America and Africa, where urbanisation is fastest.

flashcards.definition: Housing built without permission on land people do not own, often from scrap materials and lacking water, sanitation and electricity.
flashcards.example: New migrants to a fast-growing city build shelters from wood and metal sheets on unused land at the city edge.

flashcards.definition: Jobs without contracts, fixed wages or legal protection — such as street selling or casual labour — common in rapidly growing cities.
flashcards.example: Selling fruit at a roadside stall to earn a daily income with no employer or pension.

flashcards.definition: The comparison between dependents (under 15s and over 65s) and the working-age population who support them.
flashcards.example: An ageing country has many elderly dependents per worker, straining pensions and healthcare.

choices: The total population of a country
The number of people per square kilometre
The number of births per year
The percentage of people living in cities
questions.explanation: Population density = population ÷ area, expressed as people per km². It allows fair comparison between crowded and empty places regardless of their size.

questions.stem: Which of these regions is most likely to be sparsely populated?
choices: A fertile river valley
A flat coastal lowland with a mild climate
A hot desert
Land near a major port
questions.explanation: Hot deserts lack reliable water and are too dry for farming, so few people can live there. Fertile valleys, mild coasts and trading ports all attract dense settlement.

questions.stem: In a population pyramid, what does a wide base indicate?
choices: A low birth rate
A high birth rate with many children
A large elderly population
More women than men
questions.explanation: The base of the pyramid shows the youngest age groups, so a wide base means many babies are being born — a high birth rate, typical of poorer countries.

questions.stem: A country has a birth rate of 34 per 1 000 and a death rate of 12 per 1 000. What is its natural increase?
choices: 22 per 1 000 (2.2% per year)
The population is decreasing
questions.explanation: Natural increase = birth rate − death rate = 34 − 12 = 22 per 1 000, which is 2.2% per year. Because births exceed deaths, the population is growing.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a PULL factor in migration?
choices: War in the home country
Drought destroying crops
Better-paid jobs in the destination city
Unemployment in the home region
questions.explanation: Pull factors are the attractions of the destination — jobs, wages, services and safety. War, drought and unemployment are push factors: negatives that drive people away from the origin.

questions.stem: A country's population pyramid is tall with straight sides and a broad top. What does this tell you about the country?
choices: It has a high birth rate and low life expectancy
It has a low birth rate and an ageing population, so it will need more healthcare and pensions
It is a poor country with many child workers
Its population is doubling every few years
questions.explanation: Straight sides and a broad top mean few births but most people surviving into old age — an ageing population. This creates a high elderly dependency ratio, so the country must plan for care homes, pensions and health services.

questions.stem: What is the main cause of urbanisation in most countries today?
choices: People moving from cities to the countryside
Rural-to-urban migration combined with natural increase among young city populations
Governments forcing people to live in cities
Falling death rates in villages
questions.explanation: Most urban growth comes from rural people migrating to cities for work and services, plus natural increase — migrants tend to be young adults who then have children in the city.

questions.stem: Why do informal settlements (shanty towns) grow on the edges of rapidly expanding cities?
choices: People prefer building with scrap materials
Population growth outpaces formal housing, and new migrants cannot afford to buy or rent legal homes
Governments require migrants to live outside the city
The land at the city edge is the most expensive
questions.explanation: When thousands of migrants arrive each month, official housing construction cannot keep up. With no affordable legal option, newcomers build their own shelters on unused land — creating informal settlements.

questions.stem: A city struggles with gridlocked traffic and smog. Which solution would best reduce BOTH problems?
choices: Building more multi-lane roads through the centre
Investing in cheap, reliable public transport and cycle lanes
Banning all residents from owning cars immediately
Moving the city's hospitals to the suburbs
questions.explanation: Good public transport and cycling infrastructure give people a real alternative to driving, cutting both congestion and exhaust emissions. More roads often just attract more cars, and an instant total car ban is impractical.

choices: The growth of megacities
People moving from cities back out to villages and smaller settlements, often commuting in to work
The demolition of city centres
Migration between two different countries
questions.explanation: Counter-urbanisation is the reverse of urbanisation — people leaving big cities for a quieter rural life while keeping city jobs by commuting or working remotely. It is common in wealthy countries.

questions.stem: What is the informal sector of a city's economy?
choices: Jobs with contracts, pensions and fixed wages
Work without contracts or legal protection, such as street selling and casual labour
Government employment in offices
Any job located outside the city centre
questions.explanation: The informal sector covers unregistered, unprotected work — street vending, day labour, waste recycling. It grows when a city's formal economy cannot provide enough jobs for all its new residents.

questions.stem: Country X has a population of 8 million in 200 000 km². Country Y has 4 million in 10 000 km². Which statement is correct?
choices: Country X is more densely populated because its total population is larger
Country Y is more densely populated: 400 people per km² compared with 40 in Country X
Both countries have the same density
Density cannot be compared between countries
questions.explanation: X: 8 000 000 ÷ 200 000 = 40 per km². Y: 4 000 000 ÷ 10 000 = 400 per km². A bigger total population does NOT mean higher density — the area matters just as much.

questions.stem: A country has a natural increase of 5 per 1 000 per year, yet its total population falls. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: The birth rate must have been misrecorded
Net migration is negative — more people are emigrating than immigrating, by more than the natural increase
Natural increase always makes the population grow
The death rate must be higher than the birth rate
questions.explanation: Total change = natural increase + net migration. Population can fall despite positive natural increase if emigration exceeds immigration by a larger amount — for example, young workers leaving to find jobs abroad.

questions.stem: A city government wants to improve an informal settlement. Which approach is most likely to succeed and why?
choices: Demolish the settlement and rehouse everyone in tower blocks far away
Ignore it — informal settlements always improve by themselves
Self-help and site-and-service schemes that provide water, sewers, electricity and legal land titles so residents can upgrade their own homes
Build a fence around the settlement to stop it growing
questions.explanation: Self-help schemes work with the community: residents keep their homes and social networks, and basic services plus legal ownership let them improve safely. Demolition destroys communities and simply moves the problem elsewhere.

questions.stem: During the demographic transition, why does population grow fastest at the stage when death rates have fallen but birth rates remain high?
choices: Because people migrate into the country at that stage
Because the large gap between many births and few deaths produces rapid natural increase
Because birth rates rise as death rates fall
Because medicine makes people have more children
questions.explanation: Natural increase is births minus deaths. When better medicine and sanitation cut deaths but traditional high birth rates persist, the gap between them is widest — so the population expands at its maximum rate until birth rates eventually fall too.
